newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Eurotunnel, banks in basic accord.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Eurotunnel, banks in basic accord.

text.p: Troubled Anglo-French Channel tunnel operator Eurotunnel Plc said on Wednesday it had agreed in principle to restructure debts of 70 billion francs ($13.55 billion) on which it has not paid interest since 1995.
It said the plan will go to the board and banks by the end of the week and expected details to be released next week, when its suspended shares would be allowed to resume trade.
The debt accord still needs approval by all Eurotunnel's bank lenders and a qualified majority of two-thirds of its 750,000 shareholders in the tunnel link between France and Britain.

Eurotunnel, which has been fighting a savage fare war with rival ferry companies since it opened in 1994, froze payments to 225 banks on its debt in September 1995, unable to cope with the loans and cost overruns incurred during construction.

"The co-chairmen of Eurotunnel, Sir Alastair Morton and Patrick Ponsolle, and the steering group of Eurotunnel's syndicate of banks consider that agreement has been reached on the basic principles of the restructuring plan which is essential for the group's financial recovery," Eurotunnel said.
The refinancing involves initially the conversion of part of the debt into equity and an issue of convertible bonds, sources close to the deal said.

Other elements are expected to include share warrants, variable rate bonds, loans convertible into equity and "stabilisation notes" which repay debt from a percentage of the cash flow, the French newspaper La Tribune Desfosses reported.
One source said "definitive elements" of an accord were in place but would be made public after the Eurotunnel board and a 24-strong group of "instructing banks" approve the plan.
He said Eurotunnel shares, suspended on Monday in Paris, London and Brussels, should resume trading by next Tuesday once the deal has been approved and the details published.

The president of the Paris commercial court said he took the initiative to persuade a reluctant Eurotunnel and its bankers to accept a court-driven mediation process which led to the breakthrough in debt negotiations.
Jean-Pierre Mattei said he was motivated by considerations of "fairness" to the shareholders and the sheer scale of the financial and legal complications if Eurotunnel failed.

"The scale of Eurotunnel is such that a failure, with its 70 billion francs (debt), an international treaty, two courts involved -- London and Paris -- would have meant a legal and financial imbroglio without precedent," he told Reuters.
"I do not believe one can or should abandon on the roadside 750,000 shareholders who placed their confidence in the banks and in a European project as extraordinary as Eurotunnel."
Morton and Ponsolle agreed the pact with six banks which represent the 225 banks in its syndicate.
But eventually each bank must ratify the complex terms and that could take months. For technical reasons, shareholders will not be able to vote on the deal until early next year.

Although Eurotunnel agreed an outline deal last May, talks became deadlocked on the pricing of the debt conversion as the company sought to protect shareholders from a massive dilution which would come from an unacceptably low price.
A Paris Eurotunnel shareholders' group said it wanted to meet the company's management in the next few days so that it could decide its position on the deal.
